newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu rank and file upset by Arafat meeting.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu rank and file upset by Arafat meeting.

text.p: Rank and file supporters of Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday the Israeli prime minister had betrayed them by shaking hands with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

Shopkeepers at Jerusalem's Mahane Yehuda public market, traditionally a bastion of support for Netanyahu's Likud party, in May celebrated his victory with back-slapping and greetings normally reserved for Jewish holidays.
On Thursday the market was down.
"Netanyahu simply has no word. His word means nothing," said watermelon vendor David Yitzhak, in front of his wooden stall still plastered with Netanyahu campaign posters.
"If he was going to meet him (Arafat) he should have said he was going to meet him, not feed us this garbage," he said.

Netanyahu, who ousted Nobel peace laureate Shimon Peres in May elections, said while campaigning he would never meet Arafat. Netanyahu ran a campaign advertisement heaping scorn on Peres for allowing Arafat, a former guerrilla leader, to lead him by the hand.
"Netanyahu said he would bring a secure peace," said a nut vendor named Avi.
"The only thing I'm secure about is that he shook the hand of a murderer," he said before spitting sunflower seeds into the street.

The first handshake between Netanyahu, 46, and Arafat, 67, relaunched stalled talks on extending self-rule. Peres, architect of the self-rule accords, called the meeting a "moral victory" for his Labour party's policies.

Netanyahu, who defeated Peres by less than a percentage point, had opposed peace deals signed by the previous government that led to Israel's handing over of parts of the West Bank and Gaza to Palestinian control.
"You see that Arab selling eggplants?" a tomato salesman said when asked how he felt about Netanyahu meeting Arafat.
"You might as well give him my cart right now," he said.
Not all in Mahane Yehuda were disappointed by the Netanyahu-Arafat summit.
"He met with Arafat because he had no choice, he had to honour agreements. If it will help bring peace, they should meet again and again," said Abraham Cohen, 54, a butcher.
